Econometrician.structural_strength: The paper carefully distinguishes remitted wages from the allocative user cost of labor and decomposes the latter into the new-hire wage and expected wage wedge in equation (1.2). It then applies the same measurement framework separately by education, links the resulting wage patterns to CPS employment outcomes, and carries those moments into a heterogeneous-worker model. This creates an unusually coherent measurement-to-model pipeline.
Econometrician.domain_audit: The descriptive evidence supports the narrower claim that estimated user costs are more procyclical for more-educated men in the NLSY79 sample. The headline causal claim about monetary policy and inequality is not yet supported by the reported identification and inference. First, the paper infers heterogeneous effects from separate group-specific impulse responses but reports no direct tests of equality across education groups and no impulse response for an inequality contrast. A significant response for one group and an insignificant response for another does not establish that their responses differ. Second, the employment result underlying the statement that monetary easing reduces employment inequality is admitted to be sensitive to the Volcker years: the introduction says that after excluding 1979–1982, monetary policy has no statistically discernible employment impact for any education group. The high-frequency alternative also produces wrong-signed employment estimates. Third, the wage outcomes are generated from estimated Mincer coefficients and forward wage strips, but the reported standard errors do not appear to propagate first-stage estimation uncertainty. This is consequential with only 29 annual wage observations and overlapping forward wage information. Consequently, the evidence currently establishes specification-dependent group-specific point estimates, not a robust causal effect of conventional monetary policy on employment or wage inequality.
Econometrician.best_case_contribution: The strongest credible contribution is a new empirical measurement result: applying the Kudlyak user-cost methodology by education reveals substantial heterogeneity hidden by representative-agent aggregation. In the reported NLSY sample, allocative wages are approximately acyclical for men with less than high school education and considerably more procyclical for college-educated men. The accompanying model usefully shows how heterogeneous wage adjustment can generate distributional welfare losses even when an aggregate representative-worker economy matches the output gap and price level.
Econometrician.minimum_viable_revision: Estimate education differences directly in a stacked specification, report impulse responses for explicit wage- and employment-inequality contrasts with joint confidence intervals, and propagate the first-stage uncertainty in the generated UCL series through an individual- or spell-level bootstrap that repeats the entire construction and local-projection procedure. Treat the Volcker sensitivity as central rather than ancillary: either demonstrate a defensible stable employment contrast across credible shock samples or remove the general claim that conventional easing reduces employment inequality. The revised abstract should distinguish the relatively robust descriptive UCL cyclicality result from the more fragile monetary-policy estimates.
Econometrician.severity_rationale: This affects a headline conclusion stated in the abstract and introduction: that monetary easing causally reduces employment inequality while increasing wage inequality. The manuscript neither tests the relevant cross-group contrasts nor obtains a robust employment response outside the Volcker episode, and its wage inference apparently conditions on estimated outcomes. Thus the central distributional monetary-policy result is in real doubt, although the problem is repairable within the existing data and empirical framework through joint estimation, full bootstrap inference, and narrower interpretation. The descriptive education gradient in UCL cyclicality can survive even if the monetary-policy claim does not.

novelty_claims.description: Measures the user cost of labor separately by educational attainment and documents that its estimated cyclicality rises sharply with education, revealing heterogeneity masked by representative-agent estimates.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: The paper extends the established Kudlyak (2014) and Basu and House (2016) user-cost methodology to NLSY education subsamples. Tables 3 and 4 report little detectable UCL cyclicality for workers with less than high school and much larger procyclicality for college-educated workers. The data and estimators are not scarce or new, but applying the measure by education supplies a genuine and economically relevant new ingredient.

novelty_claims.description: Introduces heterogeneous wage rigidity across worker varieties into a standard New Keynesian environment and derives an output-gap-equivalent representative worker while showing that heterogeneous workers can experience larger and unequally distributed welfare losses.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: Sections 6.1–6.5 derive equal earnings elasticities under Cobb-Douglas production, define the representative wage elasticity in equation (6.5), and use a Galí et al. (2007)-style welfare calculation. This is a nontrivial heterogeneous-worker extension, although it combines established production, New Keynesian, and welfare-accounting elements rather than introducing a fundamentally new identification method or model class.

novelty_claims.description: Argues that conventional monetary easing trades lower employment inequality against higher wage inequality and that policy should place greater weight on unemployment among less-educated workers.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: The policy claim is explicit in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. Its novelty is bounded because it is an implication of the empirical and calibrated-model exercises rather than an independently identified optimal-policy result, and the employment component is sensitive to excluding 1979–1982.

insight_assessment.description: The manuscript offers useful economic intuition connecting employment-relationship durability, the expected wage wedge, education-specific wage flexibility, and distributional welfare. The argument is generally coherent, but it sometimes moves too quickly from separate group estimates to inequality and optimal-policy conclusions, obscuring the distinction between measured heterogeneity, statistically established differences, and model-dependent welfare implications.
insight_assessment.supporting_evidence: Equation (1.2) provides a clear organizing decomposition, Sections 3–5 move from tenure to wage cyclicality and policy responses, and Section 6 links those facts to welfare. However, the headline inequality statements are not accompanied by direct inequality estimands or cross-group hypothesis tests, while the conclusion recommends weighting education-specific unemployment gaps without presenting an estimated optimal rule.

Econometrician.layman_translation: The paper has a valuable finding that wages relevant to hiring and firing appear to move much more with the business cycle for college-educated workers than for workers with little education. But it has not yet shown convincingly that Federal Reserve actions cause inequality to move in the claimed directions. The graphs estimate each education group separately without testing whether the groups truly differ, and the employment finding largely disappears when the unusual Volcker-era years are removed. Better joint statistical tests and uncertainty calculations are needed before drawing the policy conclusion.
Econometrician.source_evidence: The abstract states that less-educated workers respond to monetary policy on the employment margin, more-educated workers on the wage margin, and that conventional easing reduces employment inequality but increases wage inequality. Figure 1 reports separate education-specific UCL responses, and Figure 2 reports separate employment responses, but the manuscript reports no cross-group equality test or direct inequality response. Footnote 3 states that after excluding the Volcker Reform, monetary policy has no statistically discernible impact on employment for any educational-attainment group. Appendix A.5 says the high-frequency Gertler-Karadi identification yields wrong-signed employment and hours responses. Tables 3 and 4 use UCL series generated from equation (4.1), while Section 5 applies annual local projections to these generated outcomes; the manuscript mentions Newey-West errors but no bootstrap or other propagation of first-stage Mincer and wage-strip estimation uncertainty. Table 3 contains only 29 annual observations.

Theorist.structural_strength: The manuscript builds a coherent empirical sequence from education-specific job durability to education-specific user costs of labor and then to heterogeneous responses to monetary-policy shocks. In particular, equation (1.2) usefully decomposes the user cost into the new-hire wage and expected wage wedge, making clear why separation rates and wage-tenure profiles may generate heterogeneity that a representative-worker estimate conceals.
Theorist.domain_audit: The central theoretical mapping is not internally complete. The manuscript defines W_v,t as the allocative wage measured by the user cost of labor, but then uses W_v,t L_v,t as contemporaneous household labor income in the budget constraint (6.1). Under the paper's motivating long-term-contract interpretation, the user cost is the marginal present value of the employer's labor cost, whereas household cash income is the remitted wage; these are explicitly allowed to differ. Consequently, the claims that earnings elasticities and therefore consumption elasticities are identical across varieties do not follow from the empirical UCL results. There is a second equilibrium problem: households maximize over L_v,t in (6.1), which gives an interior labor-supply condition equating the real wage to the marginal rate of substitution, while firms independently choose labor demand and the discussion additionally imposes heterogeneous wage rigidity. No wage-setting, bargaining, rationing, or labor-clearing mechanism reconciles these conditions. Finally, the monetary-policy and optimal-policy conclusions are asserted without a fully specified monetary equilibrium or policymaker problem. These are substantive proof and equilibrium gaps rather than merely missing exposition because the excess-welfare-loss result and its incidence depend on the invalid earnings-to-consumption mapping.
Theorist.best_case_contribution: The strongest credible contribution is a new empirical measurement result: applying the established user-cost methodology separately by education reveals that aggregate UCL procyclicality is concentrated among highly educated workers, while less-educated workers adjust more through employment. This is a meaningful qualification of representative-worker interpretations of wage rigidity. A properly completed model could then show how heterogeneous allocative-wage rigidity produces distributional welfare effects even when aggregate output and prices match those of a suitably constructed representative-worker economy.
Theorist.minimum_viable_revision: Separate the allocative labor cost from remitted compensation throughout the model. Specify a contract or wage-setting mechanism that determines both objects, state who chooses employment and how labor markets clear when wages are rigid, and define asset ownership and dividend allocation without duplicating aggregate profits. Then prove the claimed equality of earnings and consumption elasticities from complete equilibrium conditions, or drop that equality and recompute welfare using the resulting variety-specific consumption processes. The paper should also either solve an explicit monetary-policy problem before recommending education-weighted unemployment targets or narrow that recommendation to a conjectural implication of the welfare accounting.
Theorist.severity_rationale: The defect affects the paper's central theoretical bridge from measured UCL heterogeneity to consumption, welfare incidence, and optimal-policy conclusions. In the model as written, an allocative present-value cost is treated as contemporaneous household earnings, and rigid wages are combined with unconstrained household labor choice without an equilibrium mechanism. Thus the headline welfare result is not established. The empirical measurement contribution can survive, and the theory can plausibly be repaired within a heterogeneous-wage New Keynesian framework, so this is a serious revision rather than an unresolved blocker.

novelty_claims.description: Documents education-specific cyclicality and monetary-policy sensitivity of the user cost of labor, with highly educated workers adjusting primarily through allocative wages and less-educated workers primarily through employment.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: The manuscript applies the Kudlyak (2014) UCL construction to education subsamples and reports sharply different coefficients in Tables 3, 4, and 6 and different monetary-policy impulse responses in Figures 1 and 2. The public NLSY and CPS data and the component methods are established, but the education-specific measurement is a genuine and policy-relevant new ingredient.

novelty_claims.description: Claims that heterogeneous wage rigidity can generate greater welfare losses than an output-gap- and price-level-equivalent representative-worker economy, with the excess loss borne by workers with more rigid wages.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: Sections 6.1-6.5 construct a two-labor-variety Cobb-Douglas environment and use Jensen's inequality and a Galí et al. (2007) welfare approximation to compare heterogeneous and representative-worker economies. This is a nontrivial extension of existing frameworks, although the equilibrium and allocative-versus-remitted wage problems currently prevent the claimed result from being established.

novelty_claims.description: Claims that conventional monetary easing reduces employment inequality while increasing wage inequality and suggests that policy should place additional weight on the unemployment gap of less-educated workers.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: The abstract and conclusion emphasize the wage-employment tradeoff, and Section 7 recommends an education-weighted unemployment target. The empirical impulse responses motivate this question, but the manuscript does not solve an optimal-policy problem or establish that the proposed weighting dominates alternative policy rules.

insight_assessment.description: The paper offers useful intuition connecting employment durability, expected wage wedges, and education-specific adjustment margins. Its empirical narrative is clear, but the theoretical section moves too quickly from firm factor demands to household consumption and welfare, obscuring missing market-clearing and contracting conditions.
insight_assessment.supporting_evidence: Equation (1.2) and the counterfactual decomposition in Table 6 make the empirical mechanism transparent. By contrast, Sections 6.2-6.5 infer equal earnings and consumption elasticities from Cobb-Douglas factor shares and Euler equations without specifying the wage-setting institution, labor-market equilibrium, remitted wages, initial wealth, or the full expected income paths required for that inference.

Theorist.layman_translation: The empirical part presents an interesting pattern: less-educated workers appear to lose jobs when policy tightens, while more-educated workers keep their jobs but experience larger changes in the long-run labor cost relevant to employers. The model is meant to show that this makes recessions especially costly for less-educated workers. However, it treats an employer's present-value cost of a worker as if it were the worker's paycheck today, even though the paper's premise is that those two quantities can differ. It also does not explain who sets rigid wages or how employment is determined when households and firms make incompatible choices. The empirical finding remains valuable, but the welfare and policy conclusions need a completed model.
Theorist.source_evidence: The manuscript defines the UCL in equation (1.1) as E_t[PDV_t-beta(1-s)PDV_t+1] and states that remitted wages may be shifted intertemporally under long-term contracts. Section 6 then says W_v,t is the allocative wage and places W_v,t L_v,t directly in the household's contemporaneous budget constraint (6.1). The household maximizes over L_v,t, but the implied labor-supply first-order condition is not stated or reconciled with the firm's factor demands or heterogeneous wage rigidity. Section 6.3 asserts that equal earnings sensitivity and common Euler-equation prices imply equal consumption sensitivity, while no contract-remittance process, initial asset distribution, complete expected income path, or precise dividend ownership rule is supplied. Section 7 nevertheless concludes that the welfare-maximizing Taylor-type rule should weight unemployment gaps and especially less-educated unemployment.

Perspective.structural_strength: The manuscript explicitly disaggregates labor-market adjustment by education rather than relying on a representative worker. The decomposition of the user cost of labor into the new-hire wage and expected wage wedge, followed by education-specific estimates and welfare calculations, is a concrete strength for studying whether aggregate stabilization conceals unequal burdens.
Perspective.domain_audit: The central distributional synthesis combines outcomes estimated for materially different populations. The wage and user-cost analysis uses the NLSY79 and explicitly states, "Following Kudlyak (2014) and Basu and House (2016), I restrict the sample to males." This is an aging cohort initially aged 14–21 in 1979. By contrast, the CPS analysis is described as covering representative U.S. workers aged 25 and older, without a corresponding male or cohort restriction. Table 7 then combines CPS employment variation by education with output elasticities recovered from the NLSY to conclude that the least educated bear much larger welfare losses. Consequently, the manuscript has not established that the wage rigidity, employment response, and welfare loss characterize one common population. Sex, age, cohort, and changing composition within education groups could alter both margins. This is not merely an external-validity caveat because the unmatched estimates are inputs to the quantitative welfare comparison and the headline statement that less-educated workers adjust through employment while more-educated workers adjust through wages.
Perspective.best_case_contribution: For men represented by the NLSY79 cohort, allocative wages appear substantially more procyclical among college-educated workers than among workers without a high-school credential. When placed alongside education-specific CPS employment patterns and a stylized heterogeneous-wage-rigidity model, the evidence suggests a potentially important tradeoff: aggregate stabilization may distribute adjustment differently across education groups, with less-educated workers bearing more employment risk.
Perspective.minimum_viable_revision: Re-estimate the CPS employment, hours, and welfare inputs on a population aligned as closely as possible with the NLSY wage sample, at minimum by sex and age and preferably by cohort, and use consistently defined education groups throughout. Recalculate Table 7 and the monetary-policy comparisons using those aligned samples. If adequate alignment is infeasible, separate the NLSY and CPS findings, remove the quantitative population-wide welfare claim, and consistently narrow the abstract, introduction, and policy conclusions to the represented male cohort and the model's conditional implications.
Perspective.severity_rationale: The population mismatch affects a central inference rather than a peripheral generalization: the manuscript combines male-cohort wage estimates with broader CPS employment estimates to calibrate education-specific welfare losses. If adjustment differs by sex, age, or cohort, the claimed wage-versus-employment contrast and the magnitude or ranking of welfare losses can change. The problem is repairable using the existing data framework through aligned sample construction and recalculation, so it warrants REVISION rather than BLOCKER.

novelty_claims.description: Documents education-related heterogeneity in the cyclicality and monetary-policy sensitivity of the user cost of labor, arguing that representative-worker estimates mask an approximately acyclical allocative wage for the least educated and a strongly procyclical wage for college-educated workers.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: The empirical contribution applies the Kudlyak user-cost methodology to education groups and reports the resulting differences in Tables 3, 4, and 6 and Figure 1. The data are public and the measurement and shock-identification methods are borrowed from cited work, but the education-specific allocative-wage pattern is a genuine and policy-relevant new empirical ingredient.

novelty_claims.description: Extends a standard New Keynesian environment to labor varieties with heterogeneous wage rigidity and limited income pooling, deriving equal earnings and consumption elasticities but unequal welfare losses across varieties.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: Section 6 adds labor varieties to a Cobb-Douglas production structure and compares the heterogeneous economy with an output-gap-equivalent representative-agent economy. This is a nontrivial synthesis of established components rather than a wholly new macroeconomic framework.

novelty_claims.description: Argues that conventional monetary easing can reduce employment inequality while increasing wage inequality and that stabilization rules should place greater weight on unemployment among less-educated workers.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: The abstract and conclusion present the employment-wage tradeoff as a principal policy implication, and Section 7 proposes education-weighted unemployment gaps. Its significance is bounded by the unmatched empirical populations and by the manuscript's own appendix evidence that employment responses are sensitive to the Volcker period and monetary-shock identification.

insight_assessment.description: The argument offers useful intuition about why longer employment relationships expose educated workers more strongly to the expected wage wedge and why wage rigidity can shift adjustment onto employment. The progression from contract durability to allocative wages, monetary-policy responses, and welfare is coherent. However, the transition from separate subgroup datasets to population-level welfare conclusions is too compressed, and the stylized labor varieties are treated as education groups without enough discussion of within-group demographic heterogeneity.
insight_assessment.supporting_evidence: Equation (1.2) clearly decomposes the user cost into the new-hire wage and expected wage wedge, while Tables 2 and 6 connect contract duration and wage-tenure sensitivity to education. Sections 6 and 7 provide the economic bridge to welfare, but Table 7 combines CPS employment data with output elasticities recovered from the differently constituted NLSY sample.

Perspective.layman_translation: The paper has an important idea: workers with less schooling may lose jobs in downturns while more-educated workers keep jobs but experience more wage adjustment. The difficulty is that the wage evidence comes only from men in one particular birth cohort, while the employment and welfare calculations use a broader population. Until those samples are made comparable, the paper cannot reliably say which education group in the overall workforce bears the larger cost.
Perspective.source_evidence: Section 2 states that the NLSY79 began with respondents aged 14–21 in 1979 and that, "Following Kudlyak (2014) and Basu and House (2016), I restrict the sample to males." Section 3 labels the CPS labor-market analysis as applying to workers aged 25 and older, and Table 1 uses CPS data without stating an analogous male restriction. Section 6 says that employment is measured at the variety level using CPS Monthly Surveys. Appendix A.8 states that output elasticities used for welfare are recovered from the NLSY, while the note to Table 7 states that unemployment and hours by education come from CPS files. The abstract nevertheless refers generally to "workers" and concludes that the excess welfare loss is borne by "the least educated."

Econometrician.referee_acknowledgment: The graph converges on a coherent assessment: the education-specific user-cost measurement is a meaningful contribution, but the monetary-policy inequality claims, quantitative welfare synthesis, and theoretical mapping require substantial repair. The econometric, theoretical, and population-alignment concerns are complementary rather than competing.

attacks.critique: The manuscript does not estimate the inequality effects that support its headline monetary-policy conclusion. It presents separate group-specific impulse responses without directly estimating cross-education differences or an inequality contrast. Statistical significance for one education group and insignificance for another is not evidence that the responses differ. This issue also affects the descriptive assertion that UCL cyclicality rises with education, since Tables 3 and 4 do not report equality tests across group coefficients.
attacks.evidence: Tables 3 and 4 report separate education-specific cyclicality coefficients, while Figure 1 reports separate monetary-policy responses. No covariance-aware test of equality across education groups, stacked interaction specification, or impulse response of a wage- or employment-inequality measure is reported. Nevertheless, the abstract concludes that easing reduces employment inequality and increases wage inequality.

attacks.critique: Inference for the wage impulse responses appears to treat the estimated UCL series as observed data, although each annual outcome is a nonlinear generated variable constructed from estimated Mincer coefficients, education-specific separation rates, and overlapping forward wage strips. Newey-West errors in the second-stage local projection do not by themselves propagate this first-stage uncertainty. With only 29 annual observations, conventional asymptotic inference is especially fragile.
attacks.evidence: Equations (4.1) through (4.3) construct the UCL from estimated coefficients and exponentiated predicted wage paths truncated at seven years. Section 5 states that local-projection standard errors follow Newey and West (1987), but it describes no bootstrap or other procedure that repeats the first-stage wage estimation and UCL construction. Table 3 confirms that the annual wage analysis contains only 29 observations.

attacks.critique: The employment component of the headline policy tradeoff is not robust over credible policy regimes. Because the manuscript itself reports that excluding the Volcker reform eliminates statistically discernible employment responses for every education group, the general statement that conventional easing reduces employment inequality is not established. The instability must be treated as central evidence rather than an appendix qualification.
attacks.evidence: Footnote 3 in the introduction states that when 1979–1982 is excluded, monetary policy has no statistically discernible impact on employment for any educational-attainment group. The abstract and introduction nonetheless state the employment-inequality result without this qualification.

defenses.argument: The model critique does not overturn the paper's narrower descriptive result that estimated education-specific UCL cyclicality differs in point estimates. The allocative-versus-remitted wage inconsistency concerns the mapping from those estimates into household income, consumption, and welfare, not the construction of the empirical UCL measure itself.

The population mismatch does not invalidate the separately reported NLSY wage facts or CPS employment facts within their respective samples. Its force is concentrated on combining those estimates into a common quantitative welfare calculation and presenting the combined result as applying generally to workers.

concessions.reason: I agree that using the allocative user cost as contemporaneous household labor income conflicts with the manuscript's own distinction between allocative and remitted wages. Without a contract, wage-setting, and market-clearing mechanism connecting those objects, equal earnings and consumption elasticities and the resulting welfare incidence are not established. This is a repairable but serious substantive flaw in the theoretical and welfare contribution.

I agree that the quantitative synthesis combines an NLSY79 male cohort with CPS outcomes for a broader age-based population without demonstrating comparability. Aligning sex, age, cohort, and education definitions is necessary before interpreting the combined wage-employment moments as characterizing a common population or using them in education-specific welfare calculations.

questions.question: Would separating remitted compensation from the allocative wage within an explicit long-term contract be sufficient to preserve the proposed welfare comparison, or does the equal-consumption-elasticity result also require additional assumptions about asset ownership, insurance, and expected lifetime income?

Would matching the CPS to male members of the NLSY79 birth cohorts provide an adequate common population for the employment comparison, even though the NLSY cohort ages substantially over the monetary-policy sample?

Econometrician.final_argument_state: The surviving contribution is a medium-novelty, medium-insight descriptive measurement result: applying the established UCL framework by education produces economically different point estimates, with greater estimated procyclicality among more-educated men in the NLSY79 sample. Execution is not yet sound for the headline causal and welfare claims. The manuscript needs direct cross-group and inequality estimands, full propagation of generated-outcome uncertainty, credible treatment of policy-regime sensitivity, population-aligned wage and employment inputs, and a model that distinguishes allocative labor costs from remitted household income. The abstract and policy discussion must meanwhile be substantially narrowed. These defects are serious but potentially repairable within a major revision, so RESUBMIT rather than reject is appropriate.

Theorist.referee_acknowledgment: The peer reviews converge on a credible descriptive contribution but identify complementary barriers to the causal, population-wide, and welfare conclusions. The econometric concerns about direct cross-group inference and generated outcomes are well founded, as is the concern that the NLSY wage sample and CPS employment sample do not represent the same population.

attacks.critique: The manuscript treats acyclicality of the real user cost of labor as restoring nominal wage rigidity as an amplification mechanism, but the reported evidence does not identify nominal rigidity. An acyclical real allocative wage can arise from nominal rigidity, real rigidity, contracting, bargaining, measurement error, or offsetting nominal wage and price movements. The empirical result is therefore consistent with, rather than evidence for, heterogeneous nominal wage rigidity.
attacks.evidence: Tables 3 and 4 study real UCL cyclicality. The introduction nevertheless says that education heterogeneity 'revives the possibility of nominal rigidities as a source of amplification' and subsequently embeds the estimates in a model with heterogeneous wage rigidity without presenting evidence that distinguishes nominal from real rigidity.

attacks.critique: The empirical UCL construction does not clearly implement the time-t conditional expectation in the defining economic object. It uses estimated realized wage strips extending as much as six years beyond the hiring date and labels them anticipated wage payments. For monetary-policy analysis, the manuscript must explain the information set under which these ex post cohort wage paths estimate expectations available at t; otherwise the estimated outcome is a realized forward labor cost rather than the allocative cost perceived when the employment decision is made.
attacks.evidence: Equation (1.1) defines UCL using E_t. Equations (4.2) and (4.3) construct the wage sequence from coefficients on realized current-date and hiring-date cells, truncate the sequence at seven years, and describe the resulting terms as projected or anticipated wages. No forecasting model, time-t information set, or rational-expectations argument connecting the full-sample realized strips to E_t is supplied in the provided methodology.

concessions.reason: I concede that separate significance statements do not establish heterogeneous monetary-policy effects. The headline inequality claim requires direct education contrasts, joint inference, and uncertainty propagation through the generated UCL construction. Footnote 3 also makes the Volcker-period sensitivity central to the employment conclusion rather than a peripheral robustness qualification.

I concede that the NLSY wage analysis is explicitly restricted to men from a particular aging cohort, whereas the reported CPS employment analysis covers a broader population. Combining these moments into a single education-specific adjustment or welfare account requires aligned samples or a transparent structural transport argument.

questions.question: Would a bootstrap that resamples workers or employment spells, reconstructs every education-specific wage strip, and then estimates stacked local projections be sufficient for both generated-outcome uncertainty and cross-group inference, or does the seven-year forward construction additionally require explicit correction for overlapping future observations?

Would restricting CPS observations by sex, birth cohort, and contemporaneous age adequately align the employment estimates with the NLSY sample, or would differential attrition and the NLSY sampling design still prevent a defensible quantitative synthesis?

Theorist.final_argument_state: The surviving contribution is a medium-novelty, medium-insight descriptive finding that estimated allocative-wage cyclicality differs substantially by education in the represented NLSY male cohort. The execution does not yet support the stronger causal claim that conventional monetary easing trades employment inequality for wage inequality: direct cross-group estimands and joint inference are absent, generated UCL uncertainty is not propagated, the employment conclusion is sensitive to the Volcker period, and wage and employment moments come from unmatched populations. In addition, the forward wage-strip construction requires a clearer link to time-t expectations, and real UCL acyclicality should not be presented as identification of nominal wage rigidity. These defects appear repairable within the broad empirical framework, but they require substantial reconstruction and narrowing before the welfare and policy conclusions can be credited.

Perspective.referee_acknowledgment: The peer reviews identify complementary barriers. The Econometrician shows that separate group-specific significance statements do not establish an inequality contrast and that generated-outcome uncertainty must be propagated. The Theorist identifies a deeper disconnect between the empirically measured allocative user cost and the wage-income object required by the model. These concerns compound the population-alignment problem in my review.

attacks.critique: The manuscript's distributional conclusion combines wage and employment estimates for noncomparable populations. The NLSY wage analysis is restricted to men from a single aging cohort, whereas the CPS employment analysis covers a changing representative population aged 25 and older without an analogous sex or cohort restriction. Education-specific differences can therefore reflect sex, age, cohort, or composition differences rather than two adjustment margins faced by the same worker populations.
attacks.evidence: Section 2 states that NLSY79 respondents were aged 14–21 in 1979 and that the analysis is restricted to males. Section 3 and Table 1 instead use CPS workers aged 25 and older, with no corresponding male or cohort restriction. Nevertheless, the abstract synthesizes the results as showing that less-educated workers respond on the employment margin and more-educated workers on the wage margin.

attacks.critique: The headline inequality interpretation is not established by reporting separate education-group responses. The relevant estimand is the response of an explicit cross-group wage or employment gap, and statistical significance in one group but not another is not evidence that the responses differ.
attacks.evidence: The abstract claims that easing reduces employment inequality while increasing wage inequality. Section 5 describes separate local projections by educational attainment, and Figure 1 presents separate confidence intervals, but the supplied manuscript reports neither a direct inequality estimand nor a joint cross-group equality test.

attacks.critique: The education-specific user-cost comparison depends on a seven-year truncation that is mechanically more consequential for the college group because its employment relationships last longer. The manuscript acknowledges possible attenuation but does not quantify whether differential truncation changes the estimated cross-group contrast or its uncertainty.
attacks.evidence: Section 4.1 truncates predicted wage strips and present values at seven years. Footnote 11 explicitly notes that this may attenuate differences because highly educated workers are more likely to have truncated spells. Yet the resulting estimates are used to characterize education-specific allocative-wage rigidity without a horizon-sensitivity exercise in the supplied text.

concessions.reason: I agree that direct cross-group contrasts and full propagation of generated-UCL uncertainty are necessary for the monetary-policy inequality claim. With only 29 annual wage observations and a UCL constructed from estimated wage strips, conventional second-stage Newey–West intervals alone do not establish the precision of the final inequality estimand.

I agree that an allocative user cost cannot simply be treated as contemporaneous remitted household wage income when the paper's motivating contract environment explicitly allows those objects to diverge. A valid welfare calculation requires a contract or wage-setting mechanism linking employer user cost, remittances, employment, income, and consumption.

questions.question: Would a stacked local projection with education interactions and a spell-level bootstrap that reconstructs every UCL series be sufficient for inference, or does the small number of annual aggregate observations require randomization or weak-identification-robust inference as well?

Can the welfare result be salvaged by explicitly introducing remitted wages and a long-term contract while retaining the paper's heterogeneous-rigidity structure, or does doing so generally eliminate the claimed equality of earnings and consumption elasticities across worker varieties?

Perspective.final_argument_state: The surviving contribution is a medium-novelty, medium-insight descriptive result: within the NLSY79 male cohort, estimated allocative-wage cyclicality appears to rise with education, and equation (1.2) provides useful intuition through the expected wage wedge. The broader execution is not yet sound. The monetary-policy inequality claim lacks direct cross-group estimands and complete generated-regressor inference; the wage and employment evidence pertains to materially different populations; and the welfare model appears to conflate allocative labor cost with remitted household compensation. Differential seven-year truncation adds a secondary measurement concern. These are repairable within a substantially revised empirical and theoretical framework, but they require more than rephrasing. The abstract and policy conclusions must be narrowed unless aligned-sample estimates, valid inequality contrasts, and a coherent contract-based welfare model support them.

Econometrician.referee_acknowledgment: The peer reviews correctly identify that the manuscript's strongest surviving contribution is descriptive heterogeneity in estimated UCL cyclicality, while its monetary-policy inequality and welfare conclusions require substantial additional support. I retain my concerns about absent cross-group tests, generated-outcome inference, and policy-regime sensitivity, and I agree with the principal theoretical and population-comparability critiques.

attacks.critique: The reported GDP regressions appear to have the opposite sign from the manuscript's interpretation. If the detrended log-real-GDP indicator is positive in expansions, the negative coefficients in Tables 3 and 4 imply countercyclical rather than procyclical wages. The manuscript must define the sign of the Hamilton-filtered component, reconcile the GDP and unemployment specifications, and correct either the estimates or the interpretation before the central descriptive result can be evaluated.
attacks.evidence: Tables 3 and 4 label the cyclical indicator as detrended log real GDP and report negative UCL coefficients for every education group, including -2.88 for college graduates after controlling for match quality. The text nevertheless describes the college UCL as substantially procyclical. By contrast, the negative unemployment coefficients are consistent with procyclicality, creating an unresolved internal sign inconsistency.

attacks.critique: The local-projection specification may condition on a post-shock aggregate outcome. Contemporaneous aggregate unemployment is included when estimating education-specific employment responses, even though aggregate unemployment is itself an outcome of monetary policy and contains the education-specific outcomes being studied. Without a timing argument showing that this variable is predetermined relative to the shock, the control can absorb part of the treatment effect and mechanically alter cross-group comparisons.
attacks.evidence: Section 5 states that the controls include contemporaneous and lagged unemployment for all workers aged 25 and older. The Romer-Romer shocks originate at policy meetings, while CPS outcomes are aggregated to quarters and wage outcomes are annual or biennial. The manuscript does not explain why same-period aggregate unemployment is predetermined under these temporal aggregations.

attacks.critique: The mapping from meeting-level monetary-policy innovations to quarterly CPS outcomes and annual or biennial NLSY wage outcomes is not specified. Different aggregation rules change both the shock estimand and the effective response horizon, while biennial survey observations further complicate the purported annual local projections. This omission prevents replication and leaves the timing assumptions underlying causal interpretation unclear.
attacks.evidence: Section 5 first defines shocks at meeting date m, then writes a local projection indexed by t, states that CPS observations are quarterly, and states that NLSY observations are yearly and biennial. It does not state whether meeting shocks are summed, averaged, assigned to survey years, or otherwise aligned with each outcome frequency.

defenses.argument: The expectation critique does not eliminate the narrower empirical fact that realized cohort wage strips differ across education groups. It instead limits interpretation of those strips as the time-t expected allocative cost. The descriptive cohort-pattern result can survive if relabeled, even if the allocative and policy interpretations require a forecasting or expectations justification.

concessions.reason: I agree that acyclicality of a real UCL does not identify nominal wage rigidity. The manuscript can describe heterogeneous real allocative-wage adjustment as consistent with heterogeneous nominal rigidity, but its current transition from the empirical result to a model specifically parameterized by nominal wage rigidity is not identified by the evidence.

I agree that realized full-sample wage strips are not automatically equivalent to expectations available when a match is formed. Because the defining UCL contains a time-t conditional expectation, the manuscript needs an explicit information-set and forecasting argument or must reinterpret its measure as an ex post realized forward user cost.

I agree that seven-year truncation is differentially consequential when separation rates and tenure distributions vary by education. The manuscript acknowledges possible attenuation but does not show horizon sensitivity or propagate uncertainty from extrapolating the omitted wage wedge, so the magnitude of the cross-education contrast remains uncertain.

I reaffirm that the NLSY male-cohort wage estimates and broader CPS employment estimates cannot be interpreted as two margins for a common population without aligned samples or a transparent transport argument.

questions.question: How exactly are meeting-level Romer-Romer shocks aggregated and aligned with quarterly CPS observations and annual or biennial NLSY wage observations?

Is the reported Hamilton-filtered GDP indicator defined as actual minus forecast or forecast minus actual, and how does that definition reconcile the negative GDP coefficients with the claim of procyclicality?

Can the authors jointly bootstrap the individual wage regressions, education-specific separation rates, nonlinear UCL construction, temporal shock aggregation, and cross-education local-projection contrasts?

Econometrician.final_argument_state: The manuscript retains a medium-novelty, medium-insight descriptive contribution: within the NLSY79 male cohort, estimated realized forward wage-cost patterns differ economically by education. Execution is not sound enough for the headline causal and welfare conclusions. Direct inequality estimands and covariance-aware cross-group tests are absent; generated-UCL uncertainty is not propagated; employment results depend centrally on the Volcker period; wage and employment samples are not population-aligned; the expectation content of the UCL is unclear; and the welfare model does not adequately distinguish allocative costs from remitted household income. In addition, the apparent GDP-sign inconsistency and unresolved temporal aggregation and control timing in the local projections must be addressed. Claims that the evidence identifies nominal wage rigidity require substantial rephrasing. These defects are serious but appear repairable within a major reconstruction, so the appropriate verdict remains RESUBMIT.

Theorist.referee_acknowledgment: The peer reviews correctly identify that the manuscript's strongest surviving result is descriptive education heterogeneity in estimated UCL cyclicality, while the headline monetary-policy inequality and welfare conclusions require substantial additional empirical and theoretical support.

attacks.critique: The welfare argument lacks a coherent mapping from the employer's allocative user cost to workers' remitted earnings and consumption. The manuscript motivates the UCL precisely by allowing intertemporal wage remittances to diverge from the allocative cost, but then states conclusions about earnings, consumption, and education-specific welfare without presenting a contract or transfer mechanism connecting these objects. Consequently, heterogeneous UCL responses do not by themselves identify contemporaneous household income or welfare incidence.
attacks.evidence: Equations (1.1) and (1.2) distinguish the present value and user cost of a labor relationship from current remitted wages, explicitly because implicit contracts can shift remittances intertemporally. The introduction nevertheless claims that the model delivers identical earnings and consumption elasticities across varieties and assigns excess welfare losses to the least educated, without supplying the required mapping between UCL, remitted income, consumption, and market clearing in the provided text.

attacks.critique: The empirical UCL construction does not establish that the estimated forward wage strips equal expectations available when employment decisions are made. Realized hiring-date and calendar-date wage coefficients estimated using the full sample incorporate future shocks and are labeled anticipated wage payments without an explicit information set, forecasting equation, or rational-expectations projection. This creates a gap between the theoretical time-t expected allocative cost and the empirical realized forward cohort cost, especially when that outcome is used in monetary-policy local projections.
attacks.evidence: Equation (1.1) defines UCL using the conditional expectation E_t. Equations (4.1) through (4.3) instead use full-sample estimates of realized wage cells extending up to six years after hiring. The methodology calls these projected or anticipated payments but provides no time-t forecasting model or argument showing that the realized strips recover E_t.

attacks.critique: Acyclicality of a real allocative wage does not identify nominal wage rigidity. It is also consistent with real rigidity, bargaining behavior, contracting, measurement error, or offsetting nominal-wage and price movements. The empirical findings may motivate a model with heterogeneous nominal rigidity, but they cannot be presented as evidence selecting that mechanism.
attacks.evidence: Tables 3 and 4 estimate the cyclicality of real UCL measures. The introduction then argues that education heterogeneity restores nominal rigidity as a source of amplification and calibrates heterogeneous wage rigidity, although no evidence separating nominal from real rigidity is reported.

defenses.argument: The absence of direct cross-group tests invalidates the headline inequality inference, but it does not erase the narrower descriptive evidence that education-specific UCL point estimates differ economically in the NLSY79 male sample. That descriptive result can survive if presented as suggestive and accompanied by appropriately cautious inference.

The mismatch between the NLSY and CPS populations primarily prevents combining wage and employment moments into a unified distributional or welfare interpretation. It does not independently invalidate the wage facts within the NLSY male cohort or the employment facts within the CPS population when each is reported with its correct population scope.

concessions.reason: Separate statistical significance by education group is not evidence that the responses differ. The policy conclusion requires direct covariance-aware cross-group contrasts or impulse responses of explicit inequality measures, together with uncertainty propagation through the generated UCL outcomes. The stated disappearance of employment significance when the Volcker reform is excluded also makes regime sensitivity central to the conclusion.

The wage and employment estimates concern materially different populations: an aging male NLSY79 cohort versus a broader CPS population aged 25 and older. Aligned samples or a transparent structural transport argument are required before interpreting the two sets of responses as adjustment margins faced by common education groups.

Because the theoretical UCL is an infinite-horizon object and survival beyond seven years is more important for college-educated workers, the fixed seven-year truncation requires quantitative horizon sensitivity. The manuscript's assertion that truncation merely attenuates the education contrast is not demonstrated for cyclical covariance or monetary-policy responses.

questions.question: What contract or wage-setting mechanism maps the education-specific allocative user cost into remitted household earnings, consumption, and welfare when remittances can be shifted intertemporally?
Under what information set and expectation-formation assumption do the full-sample realized wage strips in equations (4.1) through (4.3) estimate E_t of future wage payments?

Theorist.final_argument_state: The surviving contribution has medium novelty and medium insight: applying the established user-cost framework by education yields economically different point estimates, with substantially greater estimated UCL procyclicality among more-educated men in the NLSY79 cohort, and the expected-wage-wedge decomposition supplies useful intuition. Execution is not yet sound for the central causal and welfare claims. Direct inequality estimands and joint inference are absent, generated-UCL uncertainty is not fully propagated, the employment result is policy-regime sensitive, wage and employment moments come from unmatched populations, and the welfare interpretation lacks a model connecting allocative labor costs to remitted income and consumption. The UCL construction also needs a defensible link to time-t expectations, while claims about nominal rigidity require substantial rephrasing. These defects are serious but appear repairable through substantial reconstruction and narrowing within the broad framework, so the appropriate verdict is RESUBMIT.

Perspective.referee_acknowledgment: The peer reviews correctly distinguish the manuscript's potentially valuable education-specific UCL measurement result from its stronger monetary-policy inequality and welfare conclusions. The principal concerns are mutually reinforcing rather than duplicative: missing cross-group estimands, incomplete inference for generated UCL outcomes, policy-regime sensitivity, unmatched wage and employment populations, and an insufficiently specified mapping from allocative labor costs to household welfare.

attacks.critique: The monetary-policy specification does not explain how meeting-level Romer-Romer shocks are mapped into the annual or biennial timing of the NLSY-derived wage outcomes. Without a stated aggregation rule and timing convention, the local-projection coefficient and horizon are not reproducible, and alternative annualizations could materially change estimates in a sample containing only 29 annual observations.
attacks.evidence: Section 5 identifies shocks at Federal Reserve meeting date m, but then writes a local projection indexed by t and applies it to yearly and biennial NLSY wage measures. The supplied methodology does not state whether meeting shocks are summed, averaged, assigned by survey year, or otherwise aligned with wage vintages.

attacks.critique: The UCL calculation exponentiates fitted log wages without documenting a retransformation correction. The resulting quantity generally estimates a conditional median or geometric mean rather than the expected wage level required by the present-value formula. This can distort education comparisons if residual dispersion varies by education, tenure, hiring vintage, or cyclical state.
attacks.evidence: Equation (4.1) estimates log wages, while equation (4.2) constructs wage levels using exp{estimated log wage} with no smearing factor or model for the conditional residual distribution. The economic object in equations (1.1) and (4.2) is a present value of expected wage payments in levels.

defenses.argument: The manuscript generally says that its evidence 'revives the possibility' that nominal rigidity generates amplification rather than claiming that real-UCL cyclicality identifies nominal rigidity. Thus, the inability to distinguish nominal rigidity from real rigidity, bargaining, contracting, or measurement error primarily requires disciplined interpretation and an explicit statement that heterogeneous nominal rigidity is a modeling assumption. It does not invalidate the descriptive UCL estimates themselves.

The absence of a common NLSY-CPS population does not invalidate each source-specific descriptive result considered separately. It specifically prevents the manuscript from treating the estimated wage and employment responses as two adjustment margins for the same population and from combining them without an explicit transport or reweighting argument.

concessions.reason: Separate group-specific significance statements do not establish heterogeneous responses or a change in inequality. The headline conclusion requires covariance-aware cross-education contrasts or direct impulse responses of defined wage and employment gaps.

Newey-West inference applied only to the second-stage local projections does not propagate uncertainty from the estimated Mincer coefficients, separation rates, nonlinear exponentiation, and overlapping forward wage strips. A bootstrap or equivalent joint procedure is especially important with only 29 annual observations.

The manuscript's own statement that excluding 1979-1982 eliminates statistically discernible employment responses makes policy-regime sensitivity central to the employment-inequality conclusion. The unqualified claim that conventional easing reduces employment inequality is therefore not established by the supplied evidence.

The realized forward wage strips are not automatically equivalent to expectations available when hiring decisions are made. Because there is only one aggregate history for each hiring date, subsequent aggregate shocks need not average out across workers. The paper must specify an information set and justify how its estimated cohort paths recover the conditional expectation in the UCL definition.

The welfare argument requires a coherent mapping from the employer's allocative user cost to remitted household compensation, employment, consumption, and utility. The manuscript's motivation expressly allows allocative and remitted wages to diverge, so treating the former as contemporaneous household labor income would not be internally consistent without an explicit contract or wage-setting mechanism.

questions.question: How are meeting-level monetary-policy shocks aggregated and dated relative to annual and biennial NLSY wage observations, and how sensitive are the impulse responses to alternative timing conventions?

Can the authors report direct impulse responses for explicit education wage and employment gaps, with a bootstrap that repeats the Mincer estimation, UCL construction, shock aggregation, and local projections?
How are retransformation bias, the seven-year truncation, and the distinction between realized forward wage paths and time-t expected wage paths handled in the education-specific UCL estimates?

Perspective.final_argument_state: The surviving contribution has medium novelty and medium insight: applying the established user-cost-of-labor framework by education yields economically different point estimates within the NLSY79 male cohort, and the expected-wage-wedge decomposition provides useful intuition for why job durability may matter. Execution is not yet sound for the central monetary-policy and welfare conclusions. Direct inequality estimands and joint cross-group tests are absent; generated-outcome uncertainty is not fully propagated; meeting-level shocks are not transparently aligned with annual wage outcomes; the employment conclusion is sensitive to the Volcker period; and the wage and employment evidence comes from materially different populations. The forward-strip expectation interpretation, log-to-level transformation, and differential truncation also require validation. Finally, the welfare analysis needs a contract-based distinction between allocative employer cost and remitted household income. Claims that the evidence supports nominal rigidity require substantial calibration because the empirical results do not identify that mechanism. These problems are serious but appear repairable through aligned samples, direct contrasts, joint inference, transparent timing and measurement checks, and a coherent theoretical mapping. The appropriate verdict is RESUBMIT.

final_report.editorial_rationale_and_integration:
Decision: MAJOR REVISION REQUIRED. The strongest credible version of the paper makes a meaningful empirical contribution by applying the user-cost-of-labor framework separately by education and relating the resulting heterogeneity to employment durability and the expected wage wedge. This measurement exercise is economically relevant and has MEDIUM novelty and MEDIUM insight: it suggests that representative-worker estimates conceal substantial differences across education groups, particularly within the NLSY79 male cohort. The manuscript also offers a promising measurement-to-model structure. However, all three reviewers recommend resubmission, and their concerns converge on substantive flaws in the headline causal and welfare claims.

The principal empirical flaw is that the paper claims effects on wage and employment inequality without estimating the relevant inequality objects. Separate education-specific coefficients and confidence intervals do not establish cross-group differences. The paper needs covariance-aware equality tests or direct impulse responses for explicitly defined education gaps. This problem is compounded by incomplete inference for the generated UCL outcomes: the UCL is a nonlinear function of estimated wage paths and separation rates, yet the reported Newey-West procedure does not appear to propagate first-stage uncertainty. This matters especially with 29 annual observations and overlapping forward wage information.

The monetary-policy design also requires reconstruction and clarification. Meeting-level shocks are not transparently mapped to quarterly CPS and annual or biennial NLSY outcomes; the timing and aggregation rule must be stated and tested. The inclusion of contemporaneous aggregate unemployment requires a defensible predeterminedness argument or a revised specification. Most importantly, the employment result is sensitive to the Volcker period: excluding 1979–1982 leaves no statistically discernible employment response for any education group, while an alternative high-frequency identification reportedly produces wrong-signed employment and hours responses. The current unqualified conclusion that conventional easing reduces employment inequality is therefore unsupported.

Several measurement issues affect even the narrower UCL interpretation. The manuscript must resolve the apparent sign inconsistency between negative coefficients on detrended log real GDP and the description of UCL as procyclical. It must explain how full-sample realized wage strips recover the time-t conditional expectations in the theoretical UCL, or relabel the object as an ex post realized forward cost. It should address log-to-level retransformation and test sensitivity to the seven-year truncation, which may differentially affect education groups because their employment durations differ.

The theoretical and welfare bridge is not complete. The manuscript motivates UCL as an employer-side allocative present-value cost that can differ from remitted wages, but then appears to use the allocative wage as contemporaneous household labor income. It does not provide the contract, wage-setting, labor-market-clearing, asset-ownership, and dividend-allocation conditions needed to map UCL into earnings, consumption, and welfare. Consequently, equal earnings and consumption elasticities across varieties, the incidence of excess welfare losses on the least educated, and the proposed education-weighted policy rule are not established. These conclusions require a completed equilibrium model or must be removed or presented as conditional conjectures.

A further substantive concern is population comparability. The wage analysis uses men from the aging NLSY79 cohort, whereas the CPS employment analysis covers a broader population aged 25 and older. Combining these estimates as two margins for the same workers and using them jointly in welfare calculations is not justified without aligned samples or a transparent transport argument. The paper should align sex, age, cohort, and education definitions where feasible; otherwise it must keep the source-specific findings separate and narrow its population claims.

The central substantial-rephrasal issue concerns nominal rigidity. Evidence on real UCL cyclicality does not distinguish nominal rigidity from real rigidity, contracting, bargaining, measurement error, or offsetting price and nominal-wage movements. Heterogeneous nominal rigidity may be used as a modeling assumption motivated by the facts, but it cannot be presented as identified by them. There are no separate minor-rephrasal issues in the record; most necessary changes are substantive or central in scope.

The defended critiques appropriately preserve the paper's narrower contribution. The theoretical defects do not by themselves invalidate the source-specific UCL estimates, and the population mismatch does not invalidate the NLSY and CPS facts when each is stated for its own sample. Likewise, absent cross-group tests do not erase economically different point estimates, though they prevent claims of statistically established heterogeneity or inequality effects. No extension request is necessary for the decision: a microfounded contract model or broader demographic analysis could be valuable future work, but the required revision should focus on validating the existing empirical objects and either completing or narrowing the welfare analysis.
final_report.official_letter_to_the_author:
Dear Author,

The paper's strongest contribution is its education-specific application of the user-cost-of-labor framework. The decomposition into the new-hire wage and expected wage wedge provides useful intuition for why employment durability may generate heterogeneous allocative-wage adjustment, and the estimates suggest economically important differences that representative-worker analysis may conceal. The effort to connect these facts to monetary-policy transmission and welfare is promising.

Our decision is MAJOR REVISION REQUIRED. The present manuscript does not yet support its central claims that monetary easing reduces employment inequality while increasing wage inequality, that the least educated bear the excess welfare loss, or that policy should place greater weight on their unemployment gap.

First, the inequality claims require direct estimation. Separate responses by education do not establish that groups differ. Please estimate covariance-aware cross-group contrasts—preferably in a stacked specification—and report impulse responses and joint confidence intervals for clearly defined wage and employment gaps. The same principle applies to the descriptive education gradient in UCL cyclicality.

Second, inference must account for the fact that UCL is generated from estimated wage equations, separation rates, nonlinear exponentiation, and forward wage strips. A suitable bootstrap or equivalent joint procedure should repeat the full construction and subsequent local projections. Given the 29 annual observations, the revised paper should be candid about precision and should examine sensitivity to overlapping forward information, retransformation from logs to levels, and the seven-year truncation.

Third, the monetary-policy design needs a complete timing description. Explain exactly how meeting-level shocks are aggregated and aligned with quarterly CPS and annual or biennial NLSY outcomes, and show that the results are not artifacts of a particular convention. Reconsider or justify contemporaneous aggregate unemployment as a control. The sensitivity to excluding 1979–1982 must be treated as central: if a stable employment-gap response cannot be demonstrated across defensible samples and specifications, remove the general claim that conventional easing reduces employment inequality. The alternative identification results should likewise be discussed transparently.

Fourth, resolve the internal sign issue in Tables 3 and 4. As presented, negative coefficients on detrended log real GDP appear inconsistent with the text's description of procyclicality, whereas the unemployment coefficients have the expected sign. Define the cyclical component precisely and correct either the estimates, labels, or interpretation.

Fifth, clarify the economic object being measured. Equation (1.1) contains a time-t conditional expectation, while the empirical construction uses full-sample realized wage strips. Supply an information-set and forecasting argument showing why these strips recover the relevant expectations, or reinterpret the measure as an ex post realized forward labor cost and adjust the claims accordingly.

Sixth, align the empirical populations. The NLSY wage analysis concerns men from a particular aging cohort, while the CPS employment analysis concerns a broader population aged 25 and older. Re-estimate the CPS outcomes for a population aligned as closely as feasible by sex, age, cohort, and education, and recompute any combined welfare exercise. If alignment is infeasible, report the two sets of findings separately and narrow the abstract and conclusions to their respective populations.

Seventh, the welfare model must distinguish the employer's allocative user cost from remitted household compensation. Please specify the contract or wage-setting mechanism, who chooses employment, how labor markets clear under wage rigidity, and how assets, profits, and dividends are allocated. Then derive the mapping to earnings and consumption and re-establish the welfare comparison. If this cannot be done, remove the claims of equal earnings and consumption elasticities, the quantitative incidence result, and the optimal-policy recommendation. A policy implication may be presented as conditional intuition, but not as a solved welfare-maximizing rule without an explicit policy problem.

Finally, revise the nominal-rigidity interpretation. Real UCL cyclicality does not identify nominal rigidity. The empirical findings may motivate a model with heterogeneous nominal rigidity, but the manuscript should state clearly that this is a modeling assumption rather than an empirically selected mechanism.

A successful revision need not preserve every current headline. The paper could make a valuable contribution by establishing a carefully inferred education gradient in UCL behavior for a clearly defined population and presenting the monetary-policy and welfare exercises only to the extent that the revised evidence and model support them.

Sincerely,
Senior Coordinating Editor
final_report.minimum_viable_revision_path:
1. Re-estimate education heterogeneity jointly: use a stacked specification or equivalent covariance-aware method, test equality across education groups, and report direct impulse responses for explicit wage and employment inequality contrasts.

2. Implement full uncertainty propagation: bootstrap or otherwise repeat the wage estimation, separation-rate estimation, log-to-level transformation, UCL construction, shock aggregation, and local projections. Address overlapping forward wage strips and the small annual sample.

3. Repair the monetary-policy design: document the exact aggregation of meeting shocks to each outcome frequency, justify or remove contemporaneous aggregate unemployment, and report sensitivity to timing conventions, the Volcker-period exclusion, and alternative identification. Drop the general employment-inequality claim if it is not robust.

4. Validate the UCL measure: resolve the GDP-sign inconsistency; explain how realized wage strips recover time-t expectations or relabel the object; apply an appropriate retransformation correction; and report horizon sensitivity around the seven-year truncation.

5. Align populations: construct CPS employment and hours measures matched as closely as possible to the NLSY sample by sex, age, cohort, and education, then recompute combined results. If this cannot be done credibly, separate the datasets' findings and remove population-wide quantitative welfare claims.

6. Rebuild or narrow the theory: distinguish allocative labor cost from remitted compensation; specify contracting or wage setting, employment determination, market clearing, asset ownership, and dividends; derive consumption and welfare implications; and solve an explicit policy problem before making optimal-rule recommendations. Otherwise retain only conditional model illustrations and remove unsupported welfare-incidence and policy claims.

7. Rewrite the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to distinguish robust descriptive evidence from fragile causal estimates and model-dependent implications. Present nominal rigidity as one possible modeling mechanism, not as identified by real-UCL evidence.
final_report.constructive_summary: The paper has a credible core: education-specific measurement of the user cost of labor may reveal heterogeneity hidden by representative-worker estimates, and the expected-wage-wedge decomposition offers useful economic intuition. Its novelty and insight are both best assessed as MEDIUM. The current manuscript overextends that core into causal inequality, welfare-incidence, and optimal-policy conclusions that are not yet established. The most productive revision is to prioritize direct cross-group estimands, joint inference, transparent timing and measurement, and population alignment. The theory should then either provide a coherent contract-based mapping from allocative costs to household welfare or be narrowed substantially. No unresolved blocker makes revision futile, but the required work is substantive rather than cosmetic.
